strengths: Strong theoretical contribution with rigorous convergence analysis using dynamical systems theory, providing the first f-divergence framework for DM unlearning
Elegant gradient analysis explaining different convergence behaviors of various f-divergences; empirically validated showing H² has bounded gradients while χ² unbounded
Comprehensive experimental design spanning multiple training regimes (500-5000 steps), concepts, and metrics (CS, CA, KID) with both qualitative and quantitative evaluation
Clear mathematical framework generalizing MSE approach to arbitrary f-divergences with derivation of closed-form expressions for multiple divergences
Theoretical guidance connecting f''(1) to convergence speed, validated empirically and explaining superior H² performance
weaknesses: Practical improvements over MSE are modest and inconsistent—H² gains often marginal (e.g., KID differences frequently small); complexity added may not justify benefits

Critical experimental gap: missing comparisons with important baselines (ESD, RECELER, FADE, DoCo) mentioned in related work but not evaluated empirically, significantly weakening claims of superiority
Limited architectural scope: experiments only on Stable Diffusion v1.4; no evaluation on other models/architectures, making generalizability claims unsupported

Gap between theory and practice: convergence analysis proves only local stability near equilibrium; Assumption B.7 is circular (requires optimal convergence as condition); theory doesn't provide clear practical guidance on f-divergence selection beyond empirical evaluation

Incomplete empirical analysis: no wall-clock time comparisons, computational overhead of min-max variational formulation not discussed, discriminator architecture choices unjustified, no statistical significance testing or error bars
Limited scope of multi-concept evaluation: Figure 6 shows only qualitative results; no quantitative analysis of sequential erasure interactions or re-enabling of forgotten concepts
Reproducibility concerns: no code repository mentioned, random seed handling unspecified, some hyperparameter choices unjustified, training time not reported
Insufficient ethics discussion for inherently ethical problem: lacks explicit success criteria for unlearning, consideration of misuse potential, or adversarial robustness analysis

strengths: Rigorous theoretical framework: Novel generalization from KL divergence to arbitrary f-divergences with sound mathematical foundation. Section 4.1's gradient analysis and Section 4.2's convergence analysis using dynamical systems theory are sophisticated and provide actionable insights (e.g., Eq. 106 relating 1/f''(1) to convergence speed).

Comprehensive technical approach: Provides both closed-form solutions for specific divergences and variational formulation for arbitrary f-divergences. Systematically treats multiple divergences and shows prior work (CAbl, DoCo) as special cases.

Strong experimental validation: Extensive evaluation across multiple concepts, iteration counts (500, 2000, 5000), and anchor strategies. Figure 2 effectively validates theoretical gradient predictions. Multi-concept sequential erasure demonstrates scalability. Honest reporting of trade-offs.

Well-executed presentation: Clear motivation, good visual aids, thorough related work positioning, and comprehensive appendices supporting reproducibility. Paper is well-organized despite technical complexity.
Practical contribution to important problem: Addresses real safety concerns in diffusion models (NSFW removal, copyright protection). Framework is general and could extend to other generative models.
weaknesses: Limited practical advantages: Empirical improvements of H² over MSE are marginal and inconsistent (Tables 3-5 show H² sometimes wins on quality preservation, sometimes loses on erasure metrics). Differences often fall within noise for CS/CA metrics, undermining claims of superiority.

Lack of practical guidance: Paper provides no clear operational guidance on which divergence to use when. Theorem 4.2 predicts H² and JS should be faster, but all variants converge within 500 steps empirically, raising questions about practical relevance of convergence bounds.

Theoretical limitations not fully addressed: (1) Only local convergence guarantees (Theorem 4.2); global convergence unknown. (2) Claim that different f-divergences yield same optimal solution (Eq. 3) needs formal justification, especially given mode-seeking vs mode-covering differences discussed later. (3) Assumptions B.6-B.8 are strong and unverified empirically.

Incomplete experimental evaluation: (1) Limited baselines—only MSE and CAbl compared; missing DoCo, AGE, RECELER despite mentioning them. (2) Single model version (SD v1.4) limits generalizability claims. (3) No robustness evaluation: can unlearned concepts be recovered via adversarial prompts or fine-tuning? (4) No human evaluation of visual quality; CLIP metrics have known biases.

Key experimental ambiguities: (1) KID metric interpretation is subjective and contentious—higher KID for erased concepts could indicate either successful destruction or collateral damage. (2) Regularization effects (prior preservation, gradient surgery) appear critical but no principled selection strategy provided across 9 variants tested.

strengths: Elegant theoretical generalization from KL divergence to f-divergences with rigorous gradient analysis (Eq. 7-8) showing distinct scaling behaviors for different divergences
Formal local convergence analysis using dynamical systems theory (Theorem 4.2) with bounds on convergence rates and clear connection to divergence choice via f''(1)
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple architectures (SD 1.4-2.1, SDXL, SD3, FLUX) and diverse tasks (style/object ablation, nudity erasure, adversarial robustness)
Consistent practical improvements: H-DMU achieves better prior preservation (Fig. 4, Tables 1-3) and superior robustness to adversarial attacks (Table 4: 0.042 vs CAbl 0.120 nudity rate)
Practical guidance on divergence selection: clear recommendations for H-DMU (quality preservation), χ²-DMU (aggressive erasure), and variational (maximum effect)
Model-agnostic framework applicable to different diffusion architectures, extensive implementation details and ablation studies (Appendix C.7)
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: primarily applies established f-divergence theory to new domain rather than developing fundamental methodology; gradient analysis and convergence results follow straightforwardly from existing theory

Theory-practice gap: convergence guarantees are local only under strong assumptions (B.6-B.8, especially Assumption B.7 on equilibrium); practical validity in high-dimensional non-convex optimization unclear
Modest empirical improvements: consistent but small gains (Table 2: H-DMU CS=0.624 vs MSE 0.635, ~1.7% difference); visual quality improvements somewhat subjective

Variational framework undermines unified narrative: acknowledged as inferior with higher KID (Section 5.3), suggesting closed-form methods strictly preferable; explanation for underperformance is hand-wavy

Incomplete divergence selection guidance: no systematic study of f-divergence-to-concept-type mapping; missing analysis of interaction with anchor concept choice; Table 14 shows high variation by anchor type without investigation
Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests despite averaging over multiple seeds; impossible to assess statistical significance of reported differences

Hyperparameter sensitivity underexplored: different learning rates/batch sizes for different models without justification (Table C.1); strong iteration count dependence (Tables 14-15) without clear guidance
Incomplete experimental comparisons: some recent baselines (AGE, FADE, SPEED) mentioned but not compared; limited head-to-head comparison with state-of-the-art DoCo

strengths: Well-motivated generalization of KL divergence to arbitrary f-divergences with clear practical motivation through gradient dynamics analysis
Rigorous theoretical contributions including local convergence analysis using nonlinear dynamical systems theory with explicit Jacobian characterization (Theorems 4.1-4.2)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple architectures (SD 1.4/1.5/2.1, SDXL, FLUX, SD3), diverse concept types, and adversarial robustness tests
Consistent empirical improvements of H-DMU over MSE baseline across multiple scenarios including style ablation, object removal, and nudity erasure
Clear practical guidance on divergence selection based on user goals (strong preservation vs. aggressive erasure)
Excellent technical execution with sound mathematical derivations and thorough implementation details enabling reproducibility
weaknesses: Problem formulation is a straightforward generalization of existing work (Kumari et al., 2023) with limited novelty in core objective function
Theoretical contributions apply existing f-divergence theory to known problems rather than developing fundamentally new theory
Local convergence analysis only addresses variational formulation, not the more practical closed-form losses widely used in experiments
Empirical improvements often modest and inconsistent (e.g., Table 1-2 show small margins; some scenarios show H-DMU underperforming on preservation)
Significant gap between theory and practice: gradient analysis and convergence bounds don't fully explain actual unlearning quality achieved
Extensive hyperparameter tuning required per scenario (learning rates vary 6e-6 to 5e-5, different step counts for different methods) raising fairness and generalization concerns
Variational framework significantly underperforms closed-form approach, undermining the general f-DMU framework narrative
Limited analysis of when to choose specific divergences beyond theoretical bounds; practical guidance on χ² vs H² selection is vague
